tier_reason: Stays C (first-party notebook). Enricher caveat correction: competitor models scored on features shifted by one (1-based libsvm training vs zero-based X_test), outputs unchecked; timing asymmetries in input handling and threads.

corrections.caveats: First-party prediction notebook (184 ms vs XGBoost 4.89 s and LightGBM 11.1 s) with no CPU model, compiler or library versions. The competitor models were trained on 1-based libsvm features (XGBoost.model num_feature 2001 never splits feature 0; LightGBM max_feature_idx=2000, Column_0 'none') while X_test has 2000 zero-based columns, so XGBoost and LightGBM were scored on features shifted by one and their outputs were never checked; CatBoost's features 0-1999 are aligned. Model shapes do not explain the 27x (XGBoost depth at most 6, mean 44.4 leaves vs CatBoost's symmetric 64 over the first 8000 trees; LightGBM mean leaf depth 8.2). The XGBoost DMatrix is built outside the timed cell, so only the LightGBM timing includes input handling, and the LightGBM thread count is never set. Training is slower than XGBoost and LightGBM on letters, airline and szilard/GBM-perf.

tier_reason: Downgraded B to C: enricher found an unreported correctness bug in the measured cwt() hot path (O1 buffer zeroed once per call, so sparse scale grids inherit earlier scales' products; the paper's and benchmark.cpp's dense 300-scale grids are unaffected, so the timings are real but measured on buggy code; uniwidth precedent). The Nature Computational Science paper was seen only as an abstract snippet.

corrections.caveats: Nature Computational Science abstract seen as a snippet only (122x and 34x). The '34-120x than all competitors' claim is contradicted by the repo's own CCWT row (10.63x; 3.8x at 10k-300); fCWT runs 8-thread float against single-thread double Rwave (Numerical Recipes four1 FFT) and Wavelib; factors use 0.37 s where the table shows 0.32 s and the benchmark folder README gives different times. Correctness: src/fcwt/fcwt.cpp zeroes the O1 buffer only once per cwt() call, so bins above each later scale's endpoint keep earlier scales' products (a pure 64 Hz tone appears in the 32/16/8 Hz rows at 96% with 1 voice per octave, 3.3% with 2 voices and Morlet(1.0); dense grids such as benchmark.cpp's 300 log scales are unaffected); odd signal lengths shift every other row by one sample via std::align; per-call leaks of the mother table and lastscalemem (#74 closed without the free). The Python notebook asks for 1-101 Hz at fs=100 (above Nyquist); the only PyPI wheel is cp310 macOS x86-64; -mavx is hard-coded. Bundles GPL FFTW, so usability is mixed.
